passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all. Is there no end to your long-winded speeches? What provokes you to continue testifying?” (verses 2-3).

If they were in his place, he says, he could speak as they do, heap up words and shake his head at them. “But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief” (verse 5).

“Even if I speak, my pain is not relieved, and if I hold back, how will it go away?” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The comforter was a recognized role in mourning. Friends came to sit with the grieving, share their sorrow and speak words that strengthened them. Job's friends began well, sitting in silence for seven days (2:13). The word for comforters is from nacham, the same word used when they first came to comfort him (2:11). Now it comes back with irony.

Shaking the head at someone was a public gesture of contempt. In verse 5 Job describes what the friends should have done instead: strengthen with the mouth and bring relief with the lips.

Verse 6 is honest about grief. Speaking does not take Job's pain away, and keeping silent does not either.
passages.later: The book's opening gave the friends' first intent: ‘they met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him’ (Job 2:11). And Paul gives the comforter's task in one line: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).
passages.asks: Job told his friends what he would have done in their place. Ask what words have actually brought you relief in grief, and what words have not. And ask whether your comfort to others strengthens them or only explains things to them.

passages.happening:
“Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family” (verse 7). Job's wasted body has become a witness against him. “His anger has torn me and opposed me; He gnashes His teeth at me” (verse 9). Men open their mouths against him and strike his cheeks in contempt. ‘God has delivered me to unjust men’ (verse 11).

“I was at ease, but He shattered me; He seized me by the neck and crushed me. He has set me up as His target; His archers surround me” (verses 12-13). He breaks Job with wound upon wound and rushes at him like a warrior.

Job has sewn sackcloth over his skin and buried his horn in the dust. His face is red with weeping, with deep shadows round his eyes, ‘yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Job's sense of being attacked by God reaches its most violent pictures here: a wild beast tearing, an attacker seizing him by the neck, a commander of archers, and, in verse 14, a besieger breaking through the walls of a city. Wound upon wound in the BSB is literally breach upon breach.

Some lines shift between he and You, speaking about God and to him, a sign of Job's turmoil. The Bible records his experience of God as his attacker without softening it.

In verse 8, Job's wasted body testifies against him, because in the friends' logic his suffering proves his guilt. Striking the cheek was a deep insult in a culture where honor was carried in the face.

Sackcloth was coarse goat-hair cloth worn in grief. Job has sewn it on, as if it had become part of him. The horn was a sign of strength and dignity, and burying it in the dust meant honor brought to nothing. Yet he still says his hands are clean and his prayer is pure.
passages.asks: Job did not soften what he felt, and he did not stop praying. Ask whether you have ever felt that God himself was against you. And ask what kept you, or could keep you, speaking to him.

passages.happening:
“O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest. Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high” (verses 18-19).

“My friends are my scoffers as my eyes pour out tears to God. Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor! For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return” (verses 20-22).
passages.hearers:
The idea that innocent blood cries out from the ground for justice goes back to Abel, and Israel's law treated innocent blood as something that had to be answered. Job asks the earth not to bury his cry.

Then, at the lowest point of the chapter, his hope rises. In chapter 9 he said there was no mediator between him and God. Here he says there is a witness in heaven. Witness, ed, is the word used in verse 8 of his body testifying against him; now a witness stands on his side. Beside it stands sahed, an Aramaic word for witness found only here in the Hebrew Bible.

The thread that began with his lament for a mediator climbs to its peak in chapter 19, where Job will say that his Redeemer lives.
passages.later: Job's cry draws on the first murder: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10).
passages.hard:
Who is the witness in heaven?

Job has just described God as his attacker, yet he says his witness is in heaven. Interpreters identify this witness in three main ways. Many think it is God himself: Job appeals from the God who seems to be against him to the God he trusts is just in the end, an appeal from God to God. Others think Job imagines a heavenly figure distinct from God, such as an angel who pleads for people. Eliphaz spoke of holy ones in 5:1, and Elihu will speak of a mediating angel in 33:23. A third view takes the witness to be Job's own cry, rising to heaven and testifying for him, which fits verse 18 and the tears of verse 20.

Verse 20 is itself difficult. The BSB reads it as Job's friends scoffing at him. Other translations take the same Hebrew to mean that his intercessor is his friend, continuing the thought of verse 19.

Christians have often read the verse in the light of Christ as advocate, while recognizing that Job could not have had Jesus in mind, and the New Testament does not quote it. The text leaves the identity open. Its force lies in Job's confidence that someone in heaven is on his side.
passages.asks: Job had no friend on earth to plead for him, and he believed he had one in heaven. Ask who pleads your case before God, as you understand it. And ask whom you could stand beside, as a witness for them, when no one else will.
